Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
The people responsible have faced no consequences
There is something wrong with me as a person

vignette: Rohan, a 49-year-old South Asian man, still remembers the night his wife's rage turned physical. He had been a military medic for over two decades, trained to remain calm under fire, but nothing could have prepared him for the blows that rained down on him in their own home. The pain was searing, but it was her words - "you're weak, you can't even protect yourself" - that cut deepest. As he lay there, helpless and humiliated, Rohan felt a part of him shatter. In the months that followed, Rohan became increasingly withdrawn. He stopped wearing his uniform, unable to bear the memories it stirred up. Exercise, once a source of comfort, now made him anxious; he would catch himself scanning for potential threats in the gym mirrors, just as he had during those long nights on patrol. Even social gatherings with friends and family felt treacherous - what if someone saw him as weak, too? Rohan began to avoid them all, citing work or fatigue as excuses. The scent of sweat or body odour would transport him back to that night, his heart racing like a jackrabbit's. He'd see his wife's face, twisted in anger, and feel the same physical pain he had endured during the beating. Rohan couldn't shake the feeling that it was happening all over again; time seemed to warp and distort whenever these memories surfaced. Sleep became an elusive luxury. Rohan would lie awake for hours, ears straining to pick up any unusual sounds - a creak of the floorboards, the rustle of leaves outside. He'd convinced himself that his wife might return at any moment, ready to finish what she started. Only in the safety of their bedroom, with the door locked and barricaded, could Rohan begin to relax. The lack of accountability gnawed at him; no charges were ever filed against his wife, and she seemed to have moved on without a care. This sense of injustice seeped into every area of Rohan's life. Nothing felt meaningful anymore - not his work, not his relationships, not even his own survival. He'd catch himself wondering what the point was, why he bothered getting out of bed in the morning. Self-doubt crept in like a thief, whispering that maybe there really was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person. Why else had this happened? What flaw in his character had made him such an easy target? Rohan struggled to articulate these feelings, even to himself; the memories and emotions remained stubbornly wordless, locked away behind a wall of pain. As the months turned into years, Rohan's isolation deepened. His wife had long since left, but the echoes of that night continued to haunt him. He knew he couldn't keep living like this - in constant fear, always on edge - and yet, he didn't know how to break free. The thought of seeking help filled him with trepidation; what if they saw him as weak, too? But something inside Rohan stirred, a spark of determination that refused to be extinguished. He took the first tentative step towards healing, hoping against hope that someone would finally listen, and understand.
